network.title: Network
network.firewallUnknown: The Windows firewall state could not be read.
network.hyperVLayer: Traffic to this distribution crosses a Hyper-V firewall that the Windows Defender Firewall window never shows. WSLPad only reads it.
network.inboundBlocked: Inbound traffic is blocked by default, so nothing on the network reaches this distribution unless a rule allows it.
network.allowInboundLabel: Open the virtual machine to inbound traffic
network.elevatedOnly: This one needs an administrator PowerShell, so WSLPad cannot put it in the Console for you and never runs it. Copy it, read it, and run it yourself — it lets inbound traffic into the whole virtual machine, not just one port.
network.dnsUnknown: The resolver configuration could not be read.
network.dnsMismatch: The servers in {{path}} are not the ones Windows hands out. WSL stopped maintaining this file when generateResolvConf was turned off, so it still lists the network it was written on.
network.dnsVerdictNoNameservers: {{path}} lists no nameserver, so every lookup fails with a temporary failure in name resolution.
network.dnsVerdictWillOverwrite: {{path}} was written by hand while generateResolvConf is still on, so WSL will overwrite it the next time this distribution starts.
network.dnsVerdictStale: generateResolvConf is off, so WSL no longer maintains {{path}}: the servers in it stay as written even after the network changes.
network.dnsVerdictTunneling: DNS tunneling is on, so lookups are answered by the Windows resolver rather than sent to the servers listed here.

network.portProxyAdmin: A rule is changed with netsh from an elevated prompt, which WSLPad cannot prepare in the Console — copy the command and run it yourself.

catalog.systemd-journald: Collects the messages every service prints and keeps them where journalctl can read them back. Part of systemd and running from boot to shutdown.
catalog.systemd-logind: Keeps track of who is logged in and of each login session, and creates the per-user runtime folder. Part of systemd and normally running.
catalog.systemd-resolved: Answers DNS name lookups for the whole system. Part of systemd, but WSL writes its own /etc/resolv.conf, so many WSL distributions leave it off.
catalog.systemd-timesyncd: Keeps the clock in step with a time server on the internet. Part of systemd; a WSL distribution takes its clock from Windows, so this often stays idle.
catalog.systemd-udevd: Creates the entries under /dev as the kernel reports devices, so programs can find disks and other hardware. Part of systemd and normally running.
catalog.systemd-networkd: Brings network interfaces up and gives them addresses. Part of systemd; WSL configures its own network instead, so most WSL distributions do not enable it.
catalog.systemd-oomd: Watches memory pressure and stops the worst affected process before the machine grinds to a halt. Part of systemd; Ubuntu enables it mainly on desktops.
catalog.systemd-user-sessions: Allows user logins once the rest of the boot has finished. Part of systemd: it does its one job at startup and then exits, which is why it shows as active (exited).
catalog.systemd-binfmt: Registers the extra executable formats listed in /etc/binfmt.d with the kernel. Part of systemd; it runs at boot and then exits. The same kernel feature is what lets WSL start Windows .exe files.
catalog.user-template: One systemd manager per logged-in user, named after the user id as in user@1000. Part of systemd; it runs your own user services while you are logged in.
catalog.user-runtime-dir-template: Creates and later removes the /run/user folder that holds one user's temporary session files. Part of systemd; it runs at login and exits.
catalog.getty-template: Shows a text login prompt on a virtual console, as in getty@tty1. Part of systemd; WSL has no virtual consoles, so it usually never starts.
catalog.serial-getty-template: The same text login prompt as getty, but on a serial port. Part of systemd and only useful when a serial console is attached.
catalog.dbus: The message bus that lets programs and services talk to each other on this machine. Shipped by freedesktop.org and used by most of the system, so it is normally running.
catalog.polkit: Decides whether a program that is not running as root may carry out a privileged action, such as installing a package. From freedesktop.org; it starts when something asks.
catalog.rsyslog: Writes the classic plain-text log files under /var/log, next to or instead of the systemd journal. Common on Debian and Ubuntu, and normally running when installed.
catalog.cron: Runs the jobs listed in crontab files at the times they specify. Shipped with Debian and Ubuntu, and normally running even when nothing is scheduled.
catalog.atd: Runs one-off jobs that were queued with the at command. Part of the at package; normally running but idle unless something is waiting.
catalog.logrotate: Rotates and compresses log files so they cannot fill the disk. Started by a daily timer rather than kept running.
catalog.man-db: Rebuilds the index behind man page searches such as apropos. Started by a daily timer; it is not a background service.
catalog.e2scrub_all: Checks ext4 filesystems held on LVM volumes for quiet corruption. Part of e2fsprogs and started by a weekly timer.
catalog.uuidd: Hands out unique identifiers to programs that need many of them at once. Part of util-linux; it starts on request and stops again.
catalog.udisks2: Mounts and unmounts removable drives for desktop programs that ask it to. From freedesktop.org and started on request.
catalog.multipathd: Manages disks that are reachable over more than one storage path. Part of multipath-tools; a server storage feature that WSL has no use for.
catalog.apparmor: Loads the AppArmor profiles that limit what individual programs are allowed to touch. Shipped by Ubuntu; it loads the profiles during boot and then exits.
catalog.ufw: Applies the firewall rules you set with the ufw command. Shipped by Ubuntu; it installs the rules at startup and then exits, so active (exited) is the normal state.
catalog.fail2ban: Reads the logs for repeated failed logins and temporarily blocks the addresses behind them. A community project that keeps running once installed.
catalog.chrony: Keeps the clock accurate by talking to time servers, as an alternative to systemd-timesyncd. In WSL the clock follows Windows, so it is rarely needed.
catalog.unattended-upgrades: Installs security updates on its own, without anyone logging in. Shipped by Debian and Ubuntu and normally running in the background.
catalog.apt-daily: Refreshes the APT package lists in the background. Started by a timer about twice a day, so it is idle most of the time.
catalog.apt-daily-upgrade: Installs the pending upgrades that unattended-upgrades is allowed to apply. Started by a daily timer, so it is idle most of the time.
catalog.packagekit: A shared interface that software centres and update tools use to install packages. From freedesktop.org; it starts when a program asks and exits afterwards.
catalog.snapd: Runs, updates and confines snap packages. Shipped by Canonical on Ubuntu; snaps are unusual inside WSL, so it is often stopped there.
catalog.snapd-apparmor: Loads the AppArmor profiles that belong to installed snap packages and then exits. Part of snapd on Ubuntu.
catalog.snapd-seeded: Waits until the snaps that ship with the system have finished installing, so services that need them do not start too early. Part of snapd on Ubuntu.
catalog.NetworkManager: Manages network connections on desktop Linux, including Wi-Fi and VPN profiles. From the GNOME project; WSL runs its own networking, so it is rarely used there.
catalog.networkd-dispatcher: Runs small scripts whenever a network interface comes up or goes down. Shipped by Ubuntu alongside systemd-networkd.
catalog.avahi-daemon: Announces this machine on the local network and finds others by their .local names. From the Avahi project; used for printer and file-share discovery.
catalog.cups: The printing system: it queues print jobs and talks to printers. From OpenPrinting; a WSL distribution normally has no printers of its own.
catalog.bluetooth: The Bluetooth stack that pairs and connects devices. From BlueZ; WSL has no direct access to Bluetooth hardware.
catalog.ModemManager: Talks to mobile broadband modems. From freedesktop.org and only useful on hardware that has one.
catalog.thermald: Watches the temperature of Intel processors and throttles them before they overheat. From Intel; on a WSL machine Windows already handles this.
catalog.gdm: The graphical login screen of the GNOME desktop. From the GNOME project and only present when a desktop is installed.
catalog.lightdm: A light graphical login screen used by several desktops. Shipped by Canonical and only present when a desktop is installed.
catalog.ssh: The OpenSSH server, which lets other machines log in to this one over the network. Debian and Ubuntu call the unit ssh; it normally runs once installed.
catalog.sshd: The same OpenSSH server as the ssh unit, under the name Fedora, RHEL and Arch use. It normally runs once installed.
catalog.ssh-agent: Holds your unlocked SSH keys for the session so you are not asked for the passphrase every time. Part of OpenSSH and runs inside your own user session.
catalog.gpg-agent: Holds your GnuPG keys and passphrases for the session. Part of GnuPG; it starts in your user session when something needs a key.
catalog.pipewire: Handles audio and screen sharing for a desktop session. It replaces PulseAudio on current distributions and runs inside your own user session.
catalog.pulseaudio: The older desktop sound server, running inside your own user session. Newer distributions use PipeWire instead.
catalog.docker: The Docker engine, which builds and runs containers. From Docker; WSL users often get the engine from Docker Desktop on Windows instead, and then this unit stays stopped.
catalog.containerd: The runtime that actually starts and supervises containers underneath Docker and Kubernetes. A CNCF project; it runs whenever those do.
catalog.podman: A container engine that runs containers without a permanent background daemon. From Red Hat; the service starts on request and stops again.
catalog.kubelet: The Kubernetes agent that starts and watches the containers assigned to this machine. Part of Kubernetes and only present when the machine belongs to a cluster.
catalog.postgresql: The PostgreSQL database server. On Debian and Ubuntu this unit is a wrapper that starts every database cluster you have configured.
catalog.postgresql-template: One PostgreSQL database cluster, named after its version and cluster as in postgresql@16-main. Debian and Ubuntu run one of these per cluster.
catalog.mysql: The MySQL database server. From Oracle; it keeps running while installed and holds your databases.
catalog.mariadb: The MariaDB database server, the community fork of MySQL. It keeps running while installed and holds your databases.
catalog.redis-server: Redis, an in-memory store used for caches, queues and sessions. It keeps running while installed.
catalog.mongod: The MongoDB document database server. It keeps running while installed and holds your collections.
catalog.memcached: A plain in-memory cache that applications use for short-lived values. It keeps running while installed.
catalog.rabbitmq-server: RabbitMQ, a message broker that carries jobs and events between applications. It keeps running while installed.
catalog.elasticsearch: Elasticsearch, a search and analytics engine. From Elastic; it keeps running while installed and reserves a lot of memory.
catalog.nginx: The nginx web server and reverse proxy. It keeps running while installed and serves whatever is configured under /etc/nginx.
catalog.apache2: The Apache HTTP server, under the name Debian and Ubuntu use. It keeps running while installed and serves the sites configured under /etc/apache2.
catalog.httpd: The Apache HTTP server, under the name Fedora, RHEL and Arch use. It keeps running while installed.
catalog.php-fpm: Runs PHP code for a web server such as nginx. Distributions put the PHP version in the unit name, as in php8.3-fpm.
catalog.ollama: Runs large language models on this machine and serves them on port 11434. From Ollama; the installer sets it to run in the background.
catalog.hermes-gateway: The Hermes gateway, which serves the Hermes dashboard and its local API. Part of a Hermes installation, usually as a service in your own user session.
catalog.tailscaled: The Tailscale client, which connects this machine to your private Tailscale network. From Tailscale; it keeps running while installed.
catalog.wsl-vpnkit: A community service that carries WSL network traffic through the Windows VPN when WSL cannot reach the network on its own. It runs only while you need it.
